Discussion

The present study aimed to: 1) provide a novel longitudinal test of within-person change in reading behaviour and reading motivation in middle childhood and early adolescence; and 2) examine how young people's reading motivation and reading behaviour are associated with later reading proficiency, and whether this is directly or indirectly influenced by their home literacy environment (HLE). Our findings showed strongest declines in both reading behaviour and reading motivation from age 11 to 13 years, which stabilised at age 14-15. The trajectories for both reading behaviour and reading motivation differed for boys and girls, as well as for higher vs lower socioeconomic (SES) backgrounds. For the second aim we found that HLE influenced reading motivation both directly and indirectly: adolescents with a stronger reading motivation at 11.5-years-of-age in turn reported to read more in their own time and performed better on our reading comprehension measure at age 12.5 years.

Turning to age-related changes in behaviour and motivation first, the decline in reading behaviour and reading motivation is in line with previous cross-sectional reports on age-related differences in these constructs (Clark et al., 2026), and the small number of longitudinal studies with these age groups (Miyamoto et al., 2020; Retelsdorf et al., 2023).

Interestingly, in line with Retelsdorf et al. (2023) our study also shows that this decline is most prominent from age 11 to 13 years. This could potentially reflect changes in priorities or reasons for reading. Between 11 to 13-years-of-age is a time when children in the UK transition from primary to secondary education, which may change their priorities and focus whilst they adjust to their new school environment and increasing independence and autonomy over their own time (e.g. Jindal-Snape et al., 2020). This is also a time in which peer influences become more and more important, and views towards reading may also change (e.g. reading may not be a socially acceptable activity; Webber et al., 2024) or when the type of reading they engage with shifts.

For instance, previous research with this age group shows young people indicate to read for many different reasons. Adolescents report to read for learning or for wellbeing reasons, such as reading for managing difficult emotions or relaxation (Clark et al., 2026), but our questionnaire did not include questions about these topics. They also indicate to prefer different modalities for different types of reading. For instance, some indicate to prefer paper when reading narrative fiction and non-fiction, whereas phones are the preferred modality to read social media, news, fanfiction or comics (Loh & Sun, 2022). Our data captures reading of books and novels and general motivation for reading (e.g. reading for enjoyment, talking about books, reading to imagine other worlds), but may not fully capture the full range or reading behaviours and motivations for reading that are relevant within this age group.

Importantly, the findings for sex and SES indicate that the change in reading behaviour and reading motivation differs for boys and girls and for higher and lower SES groups. Whilst overall, our data suggest the decline stabilises at age 14, when examining trajectories separately for boys and girls, we can see that rather than trajectories levelling off, the trajectories diverge for boys and girls in our study. The most prominent pattern is of an increase in reading behaviours and reading motivation for girls from age 13.5 years onwards, contrasting with an ongoing decline for boys. These findings resonate with wider concerns around boys engaging less with volitional reading than girls (Jabbar & Warreich, 2023; McGeown, 2015; Steinmann & Strietholt, 2025). The SES related differences on the other hand, seem to be mostly due to a stronger decline in reading behaviour and reading motivation for the higher SES group after age 12.5 years. Unlike previous studies, that only followed young people up to age 12 (Becker & McElvany, 2018) or 14 (Kolic-Vehovec et al., 2014), our data shows that group differences can emerge after this age. This highlights the importance of following reading motivations and reading behaviours across childhood and adolescence to gain a better understanding of how reading behaviours and reading motivation change across different individual characteristics and backgrounds and what implications this might have for policy and intervention.

The role of the home environment in reading behaviours, motivation and reading outcomes As for the second aim, examining the role of the HLE in young people's reading behaviours, motivation and ability, our findings showed that both the HLE and young people's own reading motivation and reading behaviours were associated with their subsequent reading comprehension abilities. Young people from richer home literacy environments reported higher levels of reading motivation, more leisure reading and performed better on the reading comprehension measure. This supports well established findings on the importance of HLE for reading motivation and reading attainments (Dong et al., 2020; Mol & Bus, 2011) and we build on this to demonstrate two novel aspects of this relationship. First, that the importance of HLE is longer lived than often thought. Although effects of HLE may be most obvious in early childhood (when children are wholly dependent on caregivers for their reading experiences), our findings show that even in middle childhood when children are reading independently, the home literacy environment is important in shaping young people's motivation for reading. Second, we uncover the mechanisms by which HLE, motivation and comprehension are associated and demonstrate both indirect and direct effects of HLE on reading comprehension.

As expected, even in middle childhood, when most have become proficient readers and gain more autonomy over what they read and how they spend their free time, the HLE plays a vital role in shaping young people's reading motivation and encouraging reading. This could be due to a continuing and cumulative effects of parents and carers providing access to reading materials, modelling their own reading behaviours and early shared reading throughout childhood, but also shaping their children's values and interests more broadly (Klauda, 2009). Yet, the HLE also shows a direct influence on comprehension ability, potentially due to the quality or quantity of language exposure (Mol & Bus, 2011), support provided by parents or carers for literacy related-activities (Dong et al., 2020; Claes et al., 2024), or perhaps this could reflect heritable components of parents own reading proficiency that we did not capture in our study (Hart et al., 2021; van Bergen et al., 2018). Our findings on the role of HLE have important implications for intervention and policy, emphasising volitional reading is not just something that should be encouraged in schools, but there is a role for parents and carers in providing an encouraging environment for reading in the home.

Limitations and future directions

We focused our longitudinal analyses of reading behaviours on time spent reading books or novels. This was based on previous research that shows book reading is the strongest driver for subsequent reading and vocabulary development, compared to other reading materials (Pfost & Heyne, 2023; Torppa et al., 2020). However, modelling changes in different types of reading young people engage in, such as non-fiction reading, online reading or reading comics could still provide a more complete picture of how reading behaviours change in middle childhood and adolescence. Whilst they might be less predictive of reading and vocabulary ability, young people report to read for many different reasons (Clark et al., 2024; Webbet er al., 2023) and reading experiences and types of reading for instance are also found to differ by sex or gender (Clark et al., 2024 McGeown, 2015).

Research in early and middle childhood shows that both parent's own reading ability and home literacy environment, as assessed by the number of books in the home, are associated with children's reading skills (van Bergen et al, 2017). Our measure of the home literacy environment does not allow us to tease apart any heritable characteristics and specific influences of the home environment, as we for instance did not assess parents' reading ability (i.e. Hart et al., 2021).

Finally, there was a large drop in participant numbers due to difficulty accessing schools during the global 2020-2021 pandemic. There is therefore a risk that the effects of sex and SES on reading motivation and behaviour trajectories are specific to the sample retained after age 12.5 years whose characteristics may not generalise. However, the differences in trajectories for this age group are unlikely to be easily explained by specific characteristics of a subsample. The pattern we found was complex, with an ongoing decline for boys alongside an increase for girls, alongside a stronger decline for the higher SES group. Nevertheless, to explore this possibility, we tested whether the smaller sample that continued to participate after age 12.5 years was still a good representation of the full sample (i.e. ensure not only higher SES schools or avid readers were retained in the study). The sample that remained during the pandemic did not differ in background characteristics or in reading motivation and reading behaviour at an earlier time point, meaning that the smaller sample retained in the study was still a good representation of the full sample.

Conclusion

We found declines in reading behaviour and reading motivation that were most prominent from age 11 to 13 years. In the UK, this is a time when students transition to secondary and adjust to a new school environment and responsibilities, if also often coincides with more autonomy over how they spend their own time. Importantly, our study shows reading behaviour and motivation increased for girls after this age, but not for boys. Our findings also emphasise the importance of regular reading of books and novels outside of school for reading proficiency. The significant contribution of the HLE indicates that encouraging reading is not just school's responsibility. Parents own attitudes towards reading, their own reading behaviours and shared reading in early literacy development help shape children's reading motivation and reading behaviour.
